problem: Earlier uses of LLMs in robotics were tied to one form factor or task, such as table-top manipulation or task planning. They were also mostly open-loop, one-shot prompts (GPT-3/Codex-style), so fixing bad behavior meant re-engineering the prompt from scratch. There were no general guidelines for prompting LLMs to control robots.
motivation: ChatGPT combines code generation, common-sense knowledge and multi-turn dialogue with long context. This could let a non-technical user stay 'on the loop' and correct robot behavior in natural language, instead of needing an engineer 'in the loop'. The authors observe that when ChatGPT is given a descriptively named high-level function library, it can turn ambiguous user intent into chains of API calls across very different robots, and even compose new primitives.
key_idea: Wrap platform-specific robot capabilities in a small, descriptively named high-level API library, describe it and the task in the prompt, and have ChatGPT write code (or step-by-step commands) that a human on the loop checks and corrects through dialogue before deploying it.
insight: The API description in the prompt is what grounds the model. Qualitative contrasts in Appendix A show this: with no API guidance, ChatGPT produces unbounded print-statement 'code'; with under-specified APIs, it hallucinates function parameters (e.g. EGGS_LOCATION); with clearly documented APIs, it produces executable call sequences and can even define new higher-level functions from them. Multi-turn dialogue works as a cheap correction mechanism: the model maps high-level text feedback (e.g. 'use get_yaw() when computing the step vector') to localized code edits. Feeding textual observations each turn can close a perception-action loop, but only for simple navigation. There is no quantitative ablation; all evidence is anecdotal.
method: High-level robot API library: descriptively named wrapper functions (e.g. detect_object, move_to, fly_to, get_position, grab/release) documented in the prompt and linked in the back-end to real perception, planning and control stacks.
Task-context prompting: the prompt states constraints, environment, current state, goals and optional solution examples, so the model reasons only over allowed functions.

Output-structure biasing: the prompt asks for a specific language, XML tags (<question>, <reason>, <command>), 'Question/Reason/Code' tags, or a numbered list, so outputs can be parsed automatically and clarification questions are elicited.

User-on-the-loop iteration: a human inspects the generated code, directly or in simulation (AirSim), gives natural-language feedback, and deploys only after iterating; this also supports curriculum-style skill building (pick → place → build logo).
Closed-loop dialogue control (Habitat): at each step, visible objects are given as text tuples <name, distance, angle>; ChatGPT answers with a single move(distance) or turn(angle) command.
Perception-in-the-loop code: ChatGPT writes exploration and object-search code that calls a YOLOv8 detector (plus depth masking when depth is provided) for object navigation in AirSim.
PromptCraft platform and AirSim-ChatGPT simulator: an open-source repository for sharing good and bad robotics prompts, plus a ChatGPT-wrapped AirSim environment for prototyping.

setting.training_data: none (training-free); zero-shot prompting with interactive human feedback
setting.observation: Varies by demo. Habitat VLN: text list of visible objects as <name, distance m, angle deg>. AirSim ObjectNav: front RGB through the YOLOv8 detector API (optionally depth). Drone/arm demos: object poses returned by get_position / an object dictionary.
setting.action_space: Generated Python code calling high-level APIs (fly_to(x,y,z), move_to(pose), grab/release, etc.). Habitat dialogue loop: move(distance m) / turn(angle deg), one command per step. AirSim ObjectNav: forward 0.1 m / turn_left or turn_right 90°.
setting.simulator: Microsoft AirSim; Habitat; real world (DJI Tello drone, 6-DoF suction-cup robot arm)
setting.privileged: Ground-truth object positions via get_position / a hand-provided object-coordinate dictionary in the drone and manipulation demos. In Habitat, object names/distances/angles are given as text (source not specified, likely GT). A human gives corrective feedback during the dialogue.

numbers_note: No quantitative results: the paper contains only qualitative case studies (dialogue excerpts, snapshots, videos). It reports no success rates or benchmark numbers.
results: The results are qualitative only. ChatGPT solves several robotics tasks zero-shot given only an API description: visual-servoing code, real Tello drone flight with clarification questions and inspection trajectories, and AirSim turbine inspection. With human text feedback it handles harder tasks: an AirSim obstacle-avoidance algorithm, curriculum-built block stacking into the Microsoft logo on a real arm, and YOLOv8-based object search in AirSim. It also completes a simple 'go to the chairs' navigation in Habitat, driven step by step through textual observations. No baselines are compared numerically.
limitations: There is no quantitative evaluation, no benchmark, no success rates, and no comparison against baselines; all evidence is cherry-picked dialogue examples.

The method relies on a human on the loop for correction and safety, and often on privileged object positions or hand-written scene descriptions; most demos are open-loop code generation rather than closed-loop control.
The textual closed-loop navigation works only for simple tasks; the authors state that more research is needed on describing scene context in text or vector form for complex environments.
